name: Quechua de Corongo

catalog_quote: Básicamente el acento recae en la primera sílaba de la palabra, pero el acento principal pasa a la penúltima sílaba de la última palabra de una oración.[19] (112) yúraχ áka-ta ȼári-mu-y píšta-shun-paχ almwersú-paχ ‘Agarra un cuy blanco (allá) para matarlo para el almuerzo’. En las palabras de cuatro sílabas o más, puede haber un acento secundario que recae en la penúltima sílaba.[20] (113) é:wankìman ‘puedes ir’ píštašùmpaχ ‘para que podamos degollar’. Las interjecciones se comportan de una manera especial pues reciben el acento en la sílaba final de la palabra.[21] (114) aȼaȼáw ‘¡ayayay!’ añañáw ‘¡qué bonito!’ [fn. 19] El acento básicamente recae en la penúltima sílaba en todas las variedades del quechua salvo en el QCG, el HS y el HZ en la parte occidental del departamento de Ancash. [fn. 21] A diferencia de muchas de las variedades centrales, el QCG no acentúa la vocal alargada por efecto de /-:/ ‘primera persona’. [p. 58] El acento en posición inicial (18c) sólo se encuentra en el QCG, HS y HZ en la parte occidental de Ancash. [p. 92] el acento recae siempre en la misma sílaba de las palabras.
world_status: statement found in an open source

[...] En las palabras de cuatro sílabas o más, puede haber un acento secundario que recae en la penúltima sílaba. new_statements.translation: Basically stress falls on the first syllable of the word, but the main stress moves to the penultimate syllable of the last word of a sentence. [...] In words of four or more syllables there may be a secondary stress that falls on the penultimate syllable. [...] Interjections behave in a special way, since they receive stress on the final syllable of the word. [fn. 19:] Stress basically falls on the penultimate syllable in all Quechua varieties except QCG (Corongo), HS (Huaylas) and HZ (Huaraz) in the western part of the department of Ancash.
new_statements.citation: Hintz, Daniel John. 2000. Características distintivas del quechua de Corongo: perspectivas histórica y sincrónica. Versión castellana: Marlene Ballena Dávila. Serie Lingüística Peruana 50. Lima: Instituto Lingüístico de Verano.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed on the first syllable (example (112): yúraq áka-ta chári-mu-y píshta-shun-paq); it is not sensitive to vowel length (the 1st-person lengthening suffix /-:/ is not stressed, fn. 21, and in native words stress 'recae siempre en la misma sílaba', p. 92). At the sentence level the main stress of the last word of the sentence moves to its penult (almwersú-paq). Hintz lists 'Ubicación del acento' as phonological rule 10, ordered after syllabification and before/around enclitic evidential attachment (pp. 113-114, 117).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Optional secondary stress on the penultimate syllable in words of four or more syllables (example (113) é:wankìman 'you can go', píshtashùmpaq); fn. 20 contrasts Huari (HR) where main stress is penult and secondary is initial (Stewart 1984a:196).
new_statements.exceptions: Interjections take final stress (achacháw '¡ayayay!', añañáw '¡qué bonito!'); when an interjection is re-categorised as a noun stress relocates (fn. 7 p. 102: [alláw] interjection vs [állo:] noun). Spanish loans keep the Spanish stressed syllable, realised as vowel length (§2.4.2 p. 60, §4.3 p. 92). Initial stress is an innovation shared only with Huaylas and Huaraz Quechua (p. 58, fn. 19).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule (first syllable) versus a phrase/sentence-level rule (penult of the sentence-final word receives the main stress); examples are sentence-internal words with initial stress and a sentence-final word with penult stress. Stress is described qualitatively (no instrumental data).
new_statements.identity_note: Hintz 2000 describes 'el quechua de Corongo (QCG)', spoken mainly in the districts of Aco, Cuzca and Corongo and also Yanac and La Pampa, province of Corongo, northern Ancash (§1.2 pp. 24-26) = Glottolog coro1247 / ISO qwa exactly; the 2020 Guía calls the same variety 'llaqwash'. Footnote 19/p. 58 state the initial-stress pattern is shared with Huaylas (HS, huay1240) and Huaraz (HZ) Quechua, unlike the rest of Ancash (penult).

sources.note: §4.4.2.5 'Ubicación del acento' p. 116 (p. 116): stress basically on the first syllable of the word; main stress moves to the penult of the last word of a sentence; in words of 4+ syllables an optional secondary stress on the penult; interjections stressed on the final syllable; fn. 19: penult stress in all Quechua varieties except QCG, Huaylas (HS) and Huaraz (HZ) in western Ancash; fn. 21: the 1st-person lengthened vowel /-:/ is not stressed in QCG. Also §2.3 p. 58 (18c 'Acento en posición inicial' only in QCG, HS, HZ), §4.3 p. 92 (in native words stress always on the same syllable), fn. 7…

sources.citation: Hintz, Daniel J. 2015. Sound change, reborrowing, and doublets: The anomalous third affricate in Corongo Quechua. Slides (59 pp.) of a paper presented at the Annual Meeting of the Society for the Study of the Indigenous Languages of the Americas (SSILA), Portland, OR, January 2015. PDF (created 2015-02-24) posted in the SSILA Presentations Archive, ssila.org.

tone.summary: Searched and read all 59 slides: the deck treats only the three affricate phonemes /ch'/, /ch/, /ts/ of Corongo Quechua and their origins (direct loans, reborrowing via Spanish, dialect contact, onomatopoeia, sound change, doublets). No mention of tone, pitch, accent or stress anywhere.
